Consider the matrices given above.
Find an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $\mathbf{x}=P\mathbf{y}$ defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x}$ to the canonical (diagonal) form $\mathbf{y}^T \! D \mathbf{y}.$
examples.worked_solution:
Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are 

$\qquad$ $\lambda_1=4, \quad$ $\lambda_2=2, \quad$ and $\quad\lambda_3=1.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For $\lambda_1=4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076285/assets/13eee082d48c56e6c7e796549eddc0185868b39841a7c5946ce9ce9e996ba553.png) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1  \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076285/assets/1e7c81e373377bd719e1bbc9e87a8c88d13f6116bcf2949897fc26246e2265d1.png)

- For $\lambda_2=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076285/assets/61311029da90b54253a552ce2198ce9193d7f343c3ab345eea25419444da00a3.png) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2  \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get

- For $\lambda_3=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem: Given the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2},$ find its canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables.
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -3 & 9\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -3 \\ -3 & 9-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda  & =10,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=10,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-10I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -3 & 9\end{aligned}]-10[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-10I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{\sqrt{1}0}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -3 & 9\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -3 & 9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}10 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]
$$
